title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
disposition_detail: The SJC ruled the case judicially out of order under OMSJC 10.6 and dismissed the complaint. It held the filing was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the complainant had first filed charges with the CPC Session against a teaching elder over whom the session lacked judicial authority. Nashville Presbytery properly treated the allegations as reports under BCO 31-2 and 34-1, investigated through its Committee on Judicial Business, and found no strong presumption of guilt. Because that was a new presbytery action rather than an answer to a complaint, only those with standing in Nashville Presbytery could complain against it; the original filer was not a member and lacked BCO 43-1 standing. The defects could not be cured under OMSJC 10.6.
first_summary: Laurie Lee Doty's complaint against Nashville Presbytery was dismissed. The SJC found she lacked standing to complain because her underlying filing was against a teaching elder and not a valid BCO 43-1 complaint; a dissent argued prior cases gave standing from the filing of charges.
summary: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

evidence_notes.identity_and_adoption: Case 2016-08, Doty v. Nashville Presbytery; SJC decision on complaint dated March 3, 2017; adopted by roll call 11 concur, 9 dissent, 2 abstain, 2 absent. Source lines 1, 13-17, 65-70; printed pp. 524-526.
evidence_notes.dispute: Complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's action after she had filed a charges document with CPC Session against a teaching elder. Presbytery treated the matter as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports and its Committee on Judicial Business found no strong presumption of guilt. Source lines 19-34, 47-57; printed pp. 524-526.
evidence_notes.outcomes_and_reasons: SJC held the case judicially out of order under OMSJC 10.6 and dismissed the complaint. Adopted reasons: the filing was not a BCO 43-1 complaint, the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder, Presbytery's investigation was a new action, and the non-member complainant lacked standing. Source lines 17, 19-34, 47-63; printed pp. 524-526.
evidence_notes.qualifications: The dissenting opinion of RE Howard Donahoe and others argued that filing charges gave standing under Lyons, Ruff, and Fordice; it is separate from the adopted SJC ruling and does not state the court's holding. Source lines 72-213; printed pp. 526-531.
evidence_notes.incorporated_decisions: The dissent cites Lyons v. Western Carolina (2010-16), Ruff v. Nashville (2009-28), and Fordice v. Pacific Northwest (2016-09), but those decisions are not incorporated adopted results in this case. Source lines 90-92, 171, 179, 202-212; printed pp. 527-531.
